To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
11 anti-human mAbs were identified to cross-react with canine cytokines, which may be useful for the identification of pathological conditions in dogs by flow cytometry or fluorescence microscopy.
11 commercially available anti-human mAbs were evaluated for cross-reactivity with canine cytokines and 11 anti-human mAbs cross-reacted with 11 canine cytokines.
the cross-reactivity of 11 commercially available anti-human cytokine monoclonal antibodies were identified and characterized for intracellular detection of canine cytokines by flow cytometry.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of a panel of anti-human mAbs that cross react with canine cytokines, and can be useful in the diagnosis of pathological conditions in veterinary medicine.
the establishment of a reliable and reproducible protocol for the identification of canine intracellular cytokine expression by flow cytometry.
the identification of human mAb cross-reacting with canine cytokines, which may be useful immunological markers for the diagnosis and monitoring of inflammatory diseases in dogs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
these 11 anti-cytokine mAbs could be used for canine intracellular cytokine staining by flow cytometry.
the 11 anti-human monoclonals that cross-reacted to canine cytokines can be used in flow cytometry and/or immunofluorescence for intracellular detection of canine cytokines.
the use of these anti-human monoclonals in dogs may be a reliable tool to evaluate the immune response in canine immunology studies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
11 anti-human mAbs can be used in veterinary studies.
11 anti-human mAbs were found to cross-react with canine cytokines, allowing their use for intracellular detection by flow cytometry.
the cross-reactivity of commercially anti-human monoclonals against canine cytokines is a promising tool for the development of immunological biomarkers.

the anti-human monoclonals can be used to detect the functional status of lymphocyte subsets in dogs.
